newsitem.title: GERMANY: Battered German mark is on its own for now.
newsitem.headline: Battered German mark is on its own for now.

text.p: Germany's Bundesbank has maintained an uncanny silence as the mark has been battered by the dollar in recent days, prompting speculation that the currency's front-line defender might be shifting its ground.

Economists said the central bank seemed unconcerned about the four pfennigs in four days appreciation of the dollar, perhaps accepting that sentiment in favour of a single European currency demands the fall and it would do little harm to the domestic economy for now.
While analysts said the mark's weakness was not yet at a critical point, they said the lack of "verbal intervention" from the central bank was out of character.

"The silence from the Bundesbank is somewhat surprising -- especially after their behaviour after the G7 meeting," said Klaus Baader, currency economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in London. "And it is also in complete contrast to the very vocal support for the yen that we're getting from the Japan."

Since a bout of comments soon after the last Group of Seven (G7) meeting in February, when Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said the dollar's rally "ought to end about now", very little has been heard from the bank on the subject of mark/dollar rates.

Indeed, when asked last weekend at a meeting of European finance chiefs in the Netherlands whether he was comfortable with the dollar's current levels, Tietmeyer's comment was simply: "Relatively speaking, it has actually become calmer".

The mark has since dropped further, hitting a four-week low against the dollar of 1.7198 on Wednesday -- far weaker even than the 1.66 per dollar rate at which Tietmeyer, and the G7, were last driven to verbal intervention.
At the same time, the yen crumpled to a 56-month low against the dollar overnight, prompting a flurry of defensive comments from Japanese finance officials.
But analysts said with the German economy failing to light any great fires on the growth front, the depreciation of the currency did not present a problem in the Bundesbank's eyes.

"Since the last peak in the dollar we have had some evidence that higher import prices do not pose a serious threat to inflation in Germany just now," said Holger Fahrinkrug, senior economist at UBS in Frankfurt. "This may also have contributed to a slightly softer stance from the Bundesbank."
Coupled with general dollar strength, the German currency is also being squashed lower by a growing feeling in Europe that monetary union (EMU) will go ahead on time in 1999.

If it does, with Germany itself struggling to meet the Maastricht entry criteria, many feel a slightly relaxed interpretation of the rules will have to be deployed -- allowing some "weaker currency" nations a good chance of a place in the first round.

Here, too, the central bank seems to be holding back on hard-line comment, perhaps beginning to accept that a broader group of countries will be on the starting line when the euro single currency is launched.
"I am in contact with the Bundesbank, and my impression is that they see all the effort other countries are making and they are prepared to appreciate that if it is credible," said Fahrinkrug.
Analysts said the Bundesbank's back seat approach was likely to remain in place for the time being, unless any sharp downward move in the mark began to emerge.
Credibility, as ever, remains key, and if the currency drops and volatility picks up, so too will the volume from the central bank.

"This Bundesbank is always worried about the pace at which things happen in the forex markets. It is not really the level, but the momentum that concerns them," said Fahrinkrug, adding that any swift move to the 1.73 marks per dollar region in the next few sessions would probably be enough to promt a few words.
Baader agreed: "If we get a short-term move to the 1.75 level, the Bundesbank might start to get a bit twitchy."
Analysts added, however, that there was always a risk of a "cry wolf" situation, when currencies are talked up or down so frequently that markets simply ignore the rabble.

"Too much verbal intervention can be, if not counterproductive, then certainly completely ineffectual," said Baader. "The sort of micromanagement we have seen at times in the past by the Bundesbank, where every one or two pfennigs sparked a comment, is not a strategy that can be held to for very long."
